newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan funds still cool on Asia after Thai package.
newsitem.headline: Japan funds still cool on Asia after Thai package.

text.p: Japanese funds, hit hard recently by losses in Asian bonds, will be wary about more bond investments in the region even though Thailand announced measures on Tuesday to boost its economy, fund managers said.

Thailand approved a series of tough measures, including suspending more than half its finance firms and cutting its current account deficit, with the goal of obtaining $12-$15 billion in loans from foreign countries and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
But fund managers reacted coolly to the news.
"It does seem as if they are taking some tough moves, which is positive. But at this point it is still too early to abandon a cautious stance, particularly in regard to bond investment," one said.

There appears to be good reason for such wariness. The value of most Asian bond funds established by Japanese investment trusts had fallen below their principal as of end-July, with losses ranging from six to 11 percent.
Some fund managers even reported that customers had cancelled millions of dollars of investments.
Funds more heavily slanted to Thailand suffered most, mainly due to the extreme plunges of its currency, but none escaped unscathed amid the general turmoil in the region.

One manager said an Asian bond fund with a high Thai weighting that his company established earlier this year saw its value slide by eleven percent to 8,872 yen ($75) per unit against a principal of 10,000 yen ($84) by the end of July.

"We were weighted strongly towards the ringgit, and luckily had very little in Thailand," said one manager, noting his company launched its first Asian bond fund only in June and that turmoil in Thai markets prior to that kept them from active investment there.

Despite this, losses were still hovering around seven percent, he added. "We are striving to recover the standard price per unit, but it's still far too early to make specific plans due to the unsettled market conditions."
Holdings of Asian bonds by Japanese funds stood around 30 billion yen ($254 million) as of the end of May, the latest figure available.
Investment trusts became particularly active in Asian bond funds last year, when they began selling them to individual investors eager for higher yields.

Funds were left particularly vulnerable to recent currency fluctuations by their failure to hedge against such moves. At one point the baht was down by more than 20 percent from its value on July 2, when it underwent a de-facto devaluation.
Although most managers said they had hedged against movements of the yen against the dollar, few had done the same with Asian currencies.
"Everybody hedged in dollar/yen, but not in the Asian currencies, which seemed a natural strategy at the time owing to their traditionally strong ties to the dollar," one said.
A few managers appeared hopeful that the measures announced Tuesday could help markets stabilise, but most said it was still far too early to judge.

"We need to see quite a bit more, both if they actually manage to carry out the measures strictly and also how markets respond," one said. Thai stocks plunged after the announcement, while the baht was holding mostly steady.

Most agreed it is unlikely they would offer Asian bond funds again soon. "Although there is some potential over the long term, we have to wait for things to settle down. It is difficult to even consider launching new bond funds for some time," one said. ($1=118 yen)
